Daniel Christopher · Independent case study for Kinaxia

Simulated case study · no real Kinaxia data

Keeping deliveries on time

I built Route & Margin to show how I’d make a dispatch decision and explain the numbers behind it. A chilled truck goes down at Trafford Park, leaving four deliveries without cover. The demo compares what the existing fleet, a spare vehicle and a spot carrier can do.

Starts the fault example with default assumptions. Saved comparisons remain available.

Explore the depot modelAn illustration of the two-depot network

A decision you can follow end to end

  1. Decide how much to pay for cover

    Start with the chilled vehicle fault. Compare reserve and carrier cover, then try a £280 carrier quote and read the updated recommendation.

  2. Trace one recovered delivery

    Compare the original plan with the revised arrival, then check which vehicle took the order.

  3. Understand a customer’s contribution

    Compare Cedar’s contribution under both cost allocations. Check whether its loss persists, then test a tariff change at fixed costs and volume.

How I’d test it with Kinaxia data

  1. Identify accounts to review

    Match a completed week of orders and tariffs to trips, credits and supplier invoices. Agree the contribution definition with Finance, then rank negative contribution and test allocation sensitivity.

  2. Investigate unexpected costs

    With Finance and Operations, trace invoices, waiting time, failed drops, load utilisation and extra cover back to delivery evidence.

  3. Recommend and measure

    Support tariff, delivery-pattern or operational changes with the findings. Review both service and contribution afterwards using the same cost basis.

This independent demonstration uses simulated orders, costs and delivery times. It does not use real Kinaxia data or establish actual account profitability.

Model assumptions and sourcesThe rules, references and limits of this simulation

The route planner checks depot, refrigeration, pallet capacity, payload and shift end. It prioritises deliveries served, then punctuality and transport cost. The map shows the sequence of stops, and replay follows estimated timings.

Contribution is earned revenue less transport, handling and service credits. Trip transport costs can be split by pallets or equally per served delivery, using largest remainders to reconcile every penny. Neither allocation establishes actual profitability. The defaults are £22 handling per served delivery, a 20% credit for late deliveries and a £45 credit for missed deliveries. The tariff test keeps volume, costs and credits fixed. The model excludes overheads, VAT and driver break rules. The geographic map uses approximate town centres, a simplified Natural Earth regional road network and illustrative connectors; road illustrations and replay do not change the model’s distances, ETAs or costs. Optional OSRM traces use a car profile, not HGV restrictions.

The design uses Outfit and takes colour cues from Kinaxia. The Qargo Planboard informed how the demo shows costs alongside service.

Understand the termsContribution, eligibility, recovered deliveries and cost allocation
Contribution
Earned revenue minus transport, handling and service credits. Overheads are excluded, so this is not net profit.
Contribution margin
Contribution divided by earned revenue, expressed as a percentage. The margin target is a review threshold.
Eligible plan
A plan that meets the chosen on-time delivery target. The recommendation ranks eligible plans by contribution.
Recovered delivery
An order that was late or unserved in the original plan and is on time in the selected plan.
Transport cost allocation
A way of sharing each trip’s unchanged cost between its served deliveries. Different assumptions can change individual customer contributions.
Service credit
A modelled revenue reduction for lateness or a charge for an unserved delivery, based on the adjustable assumptions.
